Satellites see the prosperity that weak governments won’t measure
The quiz Ajay Shah lost, and a lesson in perseverance

brief.head: Wrong prescription
brief.text: Critics of Big Tech describe addiction machines and echo chambers correctly, Amit Varma said, but state control of algorithms would one day fall to the worst possible person. {036-C04}

brief.head: Tyrants count heads
brief.text: Early states wanted people to tax and conscript, not territory, Ajay Shah said: “what every tyrant wants is more people”. So people voted with their feet. {036-C06}

brief.head: Fame is a curse
brief.text: Put any field under the microscope, Ajay Shah said, and what famous people loudly say turns out to be wrong. Correlations, carefully read, are a path to insight. {036-C10}

brief.head: The 60 per cent fix
brief.text: A good state intervention, Ajay Shah said, gets the job substantively done, perhaps only 60 per cent, with the least coercion, assuming realistic state capacity, or rather incapacity. {036-C11}

brief.head: Dear younger me
brief.text: Imagine sending a letter by time machine to your younger self, Ajay Shah suggested. Ego insists you did everything right; hindsight shows almost everything could have been done better. {036-C16}

thought.text: The highest superpower is the ability to keep going.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, advising idealists to pace themselves rather than burn out

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how change really happens
lead.head: Slow and steady wins the republic
body: Amit Varma needed his coffee first. Then he picked up a question left over from the hosts’ episode on India’s reformers: what kept those people fighting for decades, with no reward in sight? And how, more broadly, does change happen?
Ajay Shah’s answer, over five chapters, was that change is slow, comes from more than one direction, and cannot be rushed.
He began by pulling apart two things Indians tend to fuse. We are “excessively statist”, he said, and say “India won the World Cup” as if the players, the people and the state were one.
“Some bloke won some sports match. There is the people of India and there is the state. It’s good to separate them.” {036-C01}
Almost all the truth, beauty and creativity lies in the people, Shah said, and so does most of the rot. If anything, he said, the state is less important than the people.
## Both ends of the market

Varma once believed policy people would achieve nothing: work on the demand side, the people, and the state would follow. He has since changed his mind and thinks both ends matter. Shah agreed that both are needed. Gay rights advanced as states followed opinion polls; opening India to the world was an elite project, because “anti-foreigner comes readily”.
## Progress on probation

Varma doubted the faith that history bends towards progress, resting as it does on a small sample of centuries. Shah judged progress over the span of a single life, and found the 20th century a grim test.
“Social and political catastrophe is always possible,” he said. {036-C05}
Democratic backsliding, he added, is now happening in country after country.
## Left to right

The state, Shah said, changes through a pipeline that runs left to right: data, research, rival solutions, public debate, expert committees, decisions and implementation. Each stage needs different knowledge, and a failure at any stage kills the reform.
“And there is no running away from this pipeline.” {036-C07}
Does it take 25 years? “Yes, but there is no other way,” Shah said. Even the 1991 trade reforms, he told a sceptical Varma, rested on decades of argument among economists.
Society moves differently: not through megaphones, Shah said, but through “quiet, careful conversations from one to another”. {036-C12} Each good conversation shifts both sides by about 10 per cent.
For the cynic who would rather play his harmonium while the world burns, Shah’s answer was self-interest. In Weimar Germany, a theory of the world told you when it was time to leave.
For idealists, his advice was to pace themselves, ask for no reward and treat the work as dharma. “We are all pebbles in the avalanche,” he said. {036-C14}
Find fellow travellers who will do honest post-mortems and tell you when you are wrong, he added.

Shah recommended James C Scott’s *Weapons of the Weak*, on why many people sensibly keep the state at a distance. Varma, stepping away from the state altogether, chose the short stories of Alice Munro.

second.label: Prehistory
second.head: Paradise lost to grain
second.deck: Ajay Shah, after James C Scott, on why farming made life worse
body: As children we are told that savage hunter-gatherers progressed to agriculture and then to industry. Modern thinking, Ajay Shah said, has turned that story around: given a choice of year to be born into, you would pick a hunter-gatherer one. {036-S04}
Hunter-gatherers were free, women were free and health was good. Male skeletons reached six feet and female ones five feet seven, heights not seen again until the 20th century. {#skeleton}

Agriculture brought disease, shrinking heights, social control and women treated as property. Grain was central to early states, whose dealings with the people were taxation and conscription. Drawing on James C Scott, Shah said many people sensibly ran away. {036-C06}

quote.text: If you had to choose a year to be born into, you would always choose a hunter gatherer period.

second.caption: the curse of agriculture

third.head: Minds change by a tenth
body: As a child, Ajay Shah believed that showing someone how Kepler’s laws follow from Newton’s would change the world at once and banish superstition.
Then came many decades of gloom, he said, in which he thought people only talk past each other, smile politely, avoid conflict and never change their minds.

Now he holds a middle view. In a zone of truth and trust, people do hear each other. Nobody admits defeat, not even in their own heart, but in time the mind mulls things over and shifts by about 10 per cent. {#tenpercent}
“I will never be honest enough to say in front of you that you were right and I was wrong,” Shah said. “Okay, this is my human frailty.” {036-S06}
third.caption: three stages of persuasion

p2.title: The long game
p2.deck: How the state, society and each of us change, as argued by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

sections.label: The first question
sections.head: India didn’t win the World Cup
sections.caption: the state and the people
body: When Indians say “India won the World Cup”, Ajay Shah said, they mix up three things: some players, the people and the state. Indians are “excessively statist”, he argued, and forget that the people matter more. {036-C01}

Almost all the truth, beauty and creativity lies in the people, he said. So does much of the rot. The basic question should be how people can build culture, associations, firms and clubs themselves, instead of running to the mai-baap sarkar.

Amit Varma answered with Bertolt Brecht’s poem *The Solution*, about leaflets declaring that the people had squandered the government’s confidence: “Would it not in that case be simpler for the government to dissolve the people and elect another?” {036-J11}
## Topsoil

India, Varma said, began by assuming change would come from the top. Ambedkar described the constitution as a mere topsoil over a deeply illiberal society, and Madhav Khosla later spoke of its pedagogic effect. It cannot work, Varma argued: many people stopped building a better society, expecting the constitution to do it. {036-C03}

He once thought policy people would achieve nothing, since the state responds to the demand of the people. Now he believes small changes at the supply end can have a massive impact. {036-C02} Shah offered two templates: gay rights advanced as states followed opinion polls, while globalisation in India was an elite, top-down project.
~ Neither host claimed primacy for either route. “I’m not trying to diss anybody,” Shah said.

quote.text: change has to come from within society, it has to come from the bottom up.

sections.label: The second question
sections.head: Don’t bank on the arc
sections.caption: whether progress is guaranteed
body: Martin Luther King said the arc of the moral universe is long, but bends towards justice. Amit Varma is no longer so sure. The optimism of Francis Fukuyama’s *The End of History?* in 1989, he said, has since reversed. {036-J14} Belief in progress rests on a small sample of centuries.

Ajay Shah granted the magic of the scientific revolution, from Newton to Maxwell, relativity and Darwin. Elsewhere the story is darker. He called the stretch from agriculture in Babylon about 5,000 years ago to liberal democracy, probably in 19th-century UK, “a dark regress”. {#babylon}
## One life as the yardstick

Shah’s preferred timescale is a single life. Take random 20-year-olds and 60-year-olds of the 20th century, he said, and for large fractions of them the rest of life went terribly. The Weimar Republic’s flowering of freedom in 1918 turned into Adolf Hitler in 1933. {#weimar}
His lesson is that social and political catastrophe is always possible. {036-C05} Dream of progress and work for it, he said, but do not slip into a “millennial fervour” that it is locked in.

~ Varma cited Thomas Jefferson on the price of liberty being eternal vigilance. Shah recalled a framer of the US constitution, whose name escaped him, who said he had given “a republic if you can keep it”. {036-J18}

quote.text: So you should never get lulled into the notion of progress. There are no guarantees.

sections.label: The state
sections.head: Seven stages, no shortcuts
sections.caption: the policy pipeline
body: How does the state change? Through a pipeline that runs from left to right, Ajay Shah said, and nobody can jump the steps. It begins with data. No amount of moral urgency can substitute for it, and a moral panic is when the state rushes through its most oppressive measures. {036-C08}

Weak states fumble or suppress their numbers, so satellites help. Lights photographed at 1.30am come from street lights, petrol stations and commercial complexes, giving a monthly map of prosperity. “The bird in the sky sees the damn truth,” he said. {036-C09}

Research then refines the “crude oil” of data into knowledge. Next comes imagining solutions to genuine market failures at the least cost in money or coercion, which he called the same thing. “Ultimately the poison is coercion.” {036-C11}
## Debate, then law

There must be rival ideas, because “when there is only one game in town, you have surely a bad thing going”. A vigorous public debate, which needs free speech, widens the Overton window; expert committees legitimise radical ideas; decisions are encoded in laws; and organisations are designed to carry them out. Skip a stage, Shah said, and the reform dies there. {036-C07}
~ Each stage needs different skills. “In a good country, elected legislators write laws,” Shah said. “In a bad country, the joint secretary writes the law.” {036-J03}

quote.text: No amount of moral fervour or urgency can substitute for data.

sections.label: Society
sections.head: One WhatsApp uncle at a time
sections.caption: quiet conversations that shift minds
body: “You have controversially said and memorably said, society changes one WhatsApp uncle at a time,” Amit Varma told Ajay Shah. “Kindly explain.” {#whatsapp}

Shah began by restating that the people matter more than the state: all the wealth, art, truth and beauty are made by the people. Varma suggested the state could always set up a commission to compose a nationalistic raga. {036-J06}

Megaphone advocacy on social media, Shah said, “gets precisely nothing done”. What changes minds is eye contact, a zone of truth and trust, and living as an example, because people do as we do, not as we say. {036-C12}
## The ten per cent rule

No one concedes an argument aloud, he said, or even privately. But given time, the mind mulls things over and moves about 10 per cent. Persuade ten people by 10 per cent on a couple of important things, and that is a great deal. {#tenpercent}
~ Varma spotted an opening. After the recording, he said, he would ask Shah for ten Diet Cokes, so that Shah, shifting by 10 per cent, would hand over one. “Isn’t that cunning of me?” {036-J04}

quote.text: Society changes in one great conversation that generates a ten percent updation for both sides at a time.

sections.label: The self
sections.head: Keep going, ask nothing
sections.caption: endurance and the long haul
body: Amit Varma quoted the line from Kashinath Singh’s *Kashi Ka Assi*, in its family-friendly version: the world is going to hell, but I’m going to play my harmonium. {036-J22}

Ajay Shah’s first answer was plain self-interest. “You may not be interested in the world, but the world is interested in you,” he said. {036-C13} In Weimar Germany, the job in 1918 was to hold off the nationalists, and in 1933 to take your loved ones and run.
## Pace yourself

Idealists burn out, Shah said, by banging their heads against “some mad bugger’s wall”. Apathy is no answer either. Treat the work as your dharma, ask for no reward, and accept defeat without bitterness. {036-C14}

Then find fellow travellers who will do honest post-mortems: celebrate successes, excoriate failures, cry together, keep going. “You have to be the person that tells me that I’m full of shit,” he said. {036-C15}

A mentor at the Ministry of Finance had a career track mapped out for Shah; he chose the world of knowledge instead. {036-S07} He has known the misery of watching his work go wrong again and again, and concluded that the world owes you nothing.
~ Varma had a quiz: who said he was not so smart, he just stayed with problems longer? Shah could not guess. It was Albert Einstein.

quote.text: Our job is to build knowledge and keep pushing and accept some good things and bad things that will come out of it

side.boxText: James C Scott’s books on early states run through the episode. In *Weapons of the Weak* and *Against the Grain*, Ajay Shah said, states emerged to tax and conscript, and many people sensibly kept them out of their lives. {036-R01}

contQuote.text: But then you just have to grow up and reconcile that the world owes you nothing and the best ideas and dreams will go terribly wrong, and that’s just how the world is.

p3.title: Stories from the long road
p3.deck: Four tales of patience, from the trade reforms to a turned-down apprenticeship

stories.start: When I think of the ninety one reforms. Even if you know some

stories.caption: the 1991 trade reforms
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s provocation, and Ajay Shah’s customs-duty reply
stories.head: An overnight reform, decades old
body: Amit Varma came armed with a provocation. The 1991 reforms, he said, happened fairly quickly and with no public consultation. Many good reforms, he suggested, had skipped the long pipeline Ajay Shah had just described.
Shah disagreed, and reached for one of his favourite examples: the removal of customs duties.

Since the 1960s, through the work of Bhagwati and Srinivasan and Manmohan Singh’s PhD thesis, economists had argued vehemently over trade barriers. On the other side, Shah said, “there were always the lefties and the nationalists”.
One by one the data came out and the research came out, and in conference after conference the reformers won the debates.
By 1991, for a whole bunch of people, the question was closed: duties had to go from 350 per cent to 5 per cent. {#duty} All that was left was how to sequence it.
“But there were actually like 20 years of investment in the early stages of the pipeline that led to that simple clarity that trade barriers have to go,” he said. {036-S01}

Not every reform had such groundwork, Shah conceded, and many of those that lacked it worked out less well. The groundwork also grows the people who carry the knowledge, he said, “because the joint secretaries don’t know much”.

~ Varma promptly imagined the episode playing on a giant screen to a hall full of protesting joint secretaries, and reminded Shah, nursing a broken ankle, that he did not even have all his joints. {#jointsecs}
stories.why: Reforms that look overnight are usually the visible tip of decades of data, research and argument. The pipeline can take 25 years, Shah said, and there is no other way. {#twentyfive}

stories.start: I want to appeal to the twentieth century and choose a correct time frame
stories.end: want us to be a little cold and careful and nervous about the world
stories.caption: the 20th century
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s stress test for the idea of progress
stories.head: A century that broke its promises
body: Pick a 20-year-old or a 60-year-old at random from the 20th century, Ajay Shah suggested, and ask how the rest of their life went. For large fractions of them, terribly.

There were two world wars, the Russian Revolution, Nazi rule and the threat of communism and nuclear war. The hope of 1989 gave way to Putin’s Russia, a near-miss in Poland and the decline of Hungary.
In China, Deng Xiaoping began a programme in 1978; in 2012 came Xi Jinping and absolutist one-man rule. {#deng} In 2022, large-scale land war returned.
~ India in 1947, with Gandhiji, Nehru, Tagore and Ramanujan, was “the star pupil” of the post-colonial world, Shah said. “And you know, look at where we’ve come.” {036-S05}
stories.why: Catastrophe is always possible, so progress should never be taken as locked in. Strive for a better world, Shah said, but stay “a little cold and careful and nervous about the world”. {#nervous}

stories.start: Our friend Deviant Shu popped a question to me in a podcast conversation
stories.end: I chose a stupid path of credentialism and the glamour of the United States
stories.caption: his biggest mistake
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, asked to name one mistake, goes back to 21
stories.head: The apprenticeship he turned down
body: Asked by Amit Varma what he would write to his 17-year-old self, Ajay Shah recalled a question a friend once put to him on another podcast, with zero notice: name one mistake you have made in your life.
He went back to age 21. Fresh out of IIT, the economist Kirit Parikh invited him to apprentice with him for a couple of years, after which he could do a PhD or whatever he wanted. {#kirit}
Shah, dazzled by the glamour of the United States and a PhD, turned him down and went abroad. In hindsight, he said, it was “the dumbest decision imaginable”.
~ “Like I could have had a couple of years apprenticing with him, like literally getting one-on-one time with him four times a week,” he said. {036-S03}

quote.text: And that would have been the greatest education in the world possible.

stories.postscript: Shah first told the story on Episode 18 of the podcast *Jack of All Knowledge*.

stories.start: so as an aside my personal journey, I thought about the new pension system
stories.end: By that time I had the knowledge of how to draft a law
stories.caption: learning to draft laws
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the craft between an idea and a law
stories.head: From spectator to draftsman
body: It is one thing to think of inflation targeting, Ajay Shah said, and another to turn it into a law. He learned the difference himself.
When the New Pension System was being made law, he understood the idea but was “clueless” about its legal scaffolding. He could only watch the drafting as a spectator. {036-S02}
By the time inflation targeting came along, he had the full legal knowledge. He could walk the whole path from monetary economics to drafting an agreement, and then a law. {#inflation}
~ That is rare, he said: most laws in India are poorly drafted, and most lawyers in India don’t know how to draft law. Drafting a good one is an “exotic skill in India”.
stories.why: Turning a good idea into reality needs a different skill at each stage of the policy pipeline. Even an economist who understood the idea had to learn the craft of legal drafting to see it through.

quiz.q: Which poet suggested a government might dissolve the people and elect another?
quiz.a: Bertolt Brecht, in his poem *The Solution*, which Amit Varma read aloud.

quiz.q: How did Ambedkar describe the constitution, in Amit Varma’s account of India’s top-down beginning?
quiz.a: As a mere topsoil: a liberal document over a deeply illiberal society.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, do tyrants want people rather than territory?
quiz.a: More people to control means more people to tax, conscript and oppress.

quiz.q: What does a satellite photograph of lights at 1.30am measure, according to Shah?
quiz.a: Prosperity, every month, at half-kilometre resolution, without relying on the government.

quiz.q: Who said he wasn’t so smart, he just stayed with problems longer?
quiz.a: Albert Einstein, whom Ajay Shah failed to guess despite Varma’s clues.

quiz.q: Whose offer of an apprenticeship did a 21-year-old Ajay Shah turn down?
quiz.a: The economist Kirit Parikh’s; Shah chose a PhD in the United States instead.
